segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not to be quickly shaken out of your senses or alarmed, whether by a spirit or by a spoken word or by a letter, as though from us, claiming that the day of the Lord has come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the sanctuary of God, proclaiming himself to be God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not remember that I used to tell you these things while I was still with you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And now you know what is restraining him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the secret power of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now restrains will do so until he is out of the way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of his coming.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The coming of the lawless one is by the working of Satan, with all power and with lying signs and wonders,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and with every kind of wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they did not accept the love of the truth so as to be saved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And for this reason God sends a delusion to work in them, so that they believe the lie,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in wickedness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers and sisters loved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and faith in the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To this he called you through our good news, so that you might obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions you were taught, whether by spoken word or by our letter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal encouragement and good hope by grace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: encourage your hearts and strengthen them in every good deed and word.

notes.note: This most likely means a prophetic utterance claimed to be inspired, delivered in the congregation. The three channels named are prophecy, ordinary spoken teaching and a letter. The words “as though from us” may apply to the letter alone or to all three; the Greek leaves this open, and the punctuation here does the same.

The Greek perfect normally means “is present” or “has arrived”, and Paul elsewhere uses the same form for “things present” as opposed to things to come. The King James rendering “is at hand” (that is, near) is hard to support from usage. Most modern translations have “has come”, though how anyone could have thought the day was already here remains debated.

The Greek sentence breaks off: it gives the condition (“unless the rebellion comes first…”) but never states the main clause. Nearly all translations supply “that day will not come” from verse 2, and that is done here.

In the period the word was used both for political revolt and, in the Greek Old Testament, for religious defection from God. “Rebellion” covers both. Whether Paul has in view a defection among God’s people or a general human revolt against God is disputed, and the definite article suggests an event the readers had already been told about.
The earliest manuscripts read “lawlessness”; many later ones read “sin”, which is the reading behind the King James Version. “Lawlessness” also fits verses 7 and 8, where the same root recurs.
“Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is destined for something. The phrase means the one doomed to destruction. The related verb appears in verse 10 as “those who are perishing”.

Greek has one word for the whole temple complex and another, used here, for the inner building where the deity dwells. Most English versions render both as “temple”; this translation uses “sanctuary” for the second. Whether Paul means the Jerusalem sanctuary literally, or uses the image for a claim to divine status, is debated.

The Greek has no object, and “him” is supplied. The restrainer is a thing (neuter) here and a person (masculine) in verse 7. Paul had explained it in person, and its identity is now unknown: proposals include the Roman empire and emperor, the preaching of the good news, an angel, or God. A minority take the verb as “hold sway” and read it as a hostile power. “Now” may also go with the participle (“what is now restraining”).

Most versions have “the mystery of lawlessness”. In the Jewish Greek of the period the word meant a secret, something hidden until disclosed, not a puzzle. Here the secret is the subject of “is already at work”: lawlessness is operating out of sight before the lawless one is openly “revealed”. “Secret power” brings out that contrast.

The wording echoes Isaiah 11:4 in the Greek version, where the coming king strikes the earth with the word of his mouth and kills the wicked with the breath of his lips. The Greek word can mean “spirit” or “breath”; the allusion settles it as “breath” here.

The verb means to strip something of its force or put it out of operation; it is not the ordinary word for destroying. The King James Version and several modern versions have “destroy”, while others have “bring to nothing” or “annihilate”. The point is that the lawless one’s power collapses at the mere appearance of Jesus.

The manuscripts are divided between two readings that differ by a single letter in Greek: “as firstfruits” and “from the beginning”. The Greek text translated here reads “firstfruits”, the first portion of a harvest offered to God. Many translations follow the other reading, and the question is not settled.

The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, including public proclamations. “Gospel” is now a purely religious term or the name of a book. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters, and versions split between “brothers”, “brothers and sisters” and “friends”.
It recurs in the Pastoral Letters for Christ’s appearing, and “appearing”, “appearance”, “manifestation” and “splendor” are all in use; one rendering is needed.
The noun and its verb παρακαλέω range over “comfort”, “encouragement”, “exhortation” and “appeal” across the New Testament, and wordplay between noun and verb is easily lost without a policy.
It recurs in Paul, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and translators vary between “sanctification”, “holiness” and “consecration”.
It is common across the New Testament, is rendered variously as “unrighteousness”, “wickedness”, “wrongdoing” and “injustice”, and its link to the δικαιοσύνη word group deserves one decision.
